    A.3 The dynamics of gradient rescaling

    We found the denominator of gradient rescaling not to be subject to much variation, whereas the batch gradient norm dynamically changes the learning rate over time. Figure 10.8 compares the evolution of ∥∇t∥ for two different radii of the k-support norm ball (with fixed k), where we compare to usual SGD training with weight decay. For both SGD and SFW, ∥∇t∥ is subject to noise and increases until 75 % of the training process, despite the continuous decrease of the train loss. In fact, the batch gradient norm is not significantly smaller than at the start of training even though the loss converges. This behavior might best be explainable by the presence of batch-normalization layers, whose interplay with weight decay has been analyzed by van Laarhoven [67] and Hoffer et al. [31]: layers preceding a batch-normalization are rescaling invariant, that is, their output remains unchanged when multiplying all parameters by a scalar; however, rescaling them results in inverse rescaling of the gradient norm in subsequent layers and iterations. Weight decay continuously decreases the scale of the parameters, and hence increases the scale of the batch gradient, where stronger decay of the former leads to stronger increase of the latter. Since in gradient rescaling the norm of the batch gradient also influences the strength of the decay of the parameters, this process has a self-accelerating dynamic. This dynamic results in larger steps toward the (sparse) vertices of the k-support norm ball, leading to a stronger decay on the previous parameter configuration, which in turn increases the robustness to pruning, making gradient rescaling the method of choice in that setting.

    A.4 Proofs of LMO constructions

    In the following, we state the missing proof of the k-support norm LMO (being a special case of the group-k-support norm) and Lemma 10.1.

    Lemma 10.3.

    Given ∇t, let vt ∈ 𝒞k(τ) = conv{v ∣ ∥v∥0 ≤ k, ∥v∥2 ≤ τ} such that

    $\begin{matrix} {{\lbrack\mathit{v}_{\mathit{t}}\rbrack}_{\mathit{i}} = \left\{ \begin{matrix} {- \mathit{\tau}{\lbrack\nabla_{\mathit{t}}\rbrack}_{\mathit{i}}/{\|\nabla_{\mathit{t}}^{{top}_{\mathit{k}}}\|}_{2}\quad} & {\textit{if}\mspace{450mu}\mathit{i} \in {top}_{\mathit{k}}(|\nabla_{\mathit{t}}|),} \\ {0\quad} & {\textit{otherwise},} \\ \end{matrix} \right.} \\ \end{matrix}$

    where ∇ttopk is the vector obtained by setting to zero all n − k entries [∇t]j of ∇t with j ∉ topk(|∇t|). Then $\mathit{v}_{\mathit{t}} \in \operatorname{arg\, min}_{\mathit{v} \in \mathcal{C}_{\mathit{k}}(\mathit{\tau})}\langle\mathit{v},\nabla_{\mathit{t}}\rangle$ is a solution to Equation (10.2).

    Proof.

    By construction, all vertices v of 𝒞k(τ) satisfy ∥v∥2 = τ and are k-Sparse, that is, ∥v∥0 ≤ k. Note that being k-Sparse includes cases where more than n − k entries are zero. The minimum of Equation (10.2) is attained at one such v. Further recall the following reformulation of the euclidean inner product:

    (10.8)$\begin{matrix} {\langle\mathit{v},\nabla_{\mathit{t}}\rangle = {\|\mathit{v}\|}_{2}{\|\nabla_{\mathit{t}}\|}_{2}\cos\left( \angle(\mathit{v},\nabla_{\mathit{t}}) \right) = \mathit{\tau}{\|\nabla_{\mathit{t}}\|}_{2}\cos\left( \angle(\mathit{v},\nabla_{\mathit{t}}) \right),} \\ \end{matrix}$

    where ∠(v, ∇t) denotes the angle between v and ∇t. This term is minimized as soon as the angle between v and ∇t is maximal. If v was not required to be k-Sparse, that is, v would be allowed to lie anywhere on the border of B2(τ), the solution would clearly be given by  − τ∇t/∥∇t∥2. However, since v is k-Sparse, the vector maximizing the angle to ∇t is the one that is closest to  − τ∇t/∥∇t∥2 but is k-Sparse at the same time. This is exactly the one claimed.  □

    Lemma 10.4.

    Given ∇t ∈ ℝn × m, let 𝒲t ∈ 𝒞kσ(τ) such that

    $\begin{matrix} {\mathcal{W}_{\mathit{t}} = \frac{- \mathit{\tau}}{{\|\mathit{\sigma}(\Sigma_{\mathit{k}})\|}_{2}}\mathit{U}_{\mathit{k}}\Sigma_{\mathit{k}}\mathit{V}_{\mathit{k}}^{\mathit{T}},} \\ \end{matrix}$

    where UkΣkVkT is the truncated SVD of ∇t such that only the k largest singular values are kept. Then $\mathcal{W}_{\mathit{t}} \in \operatorname{arg\, min}_{\mathit{v} \in \mathcal{C}_{\mathit{k}}^{\mathit{\sigma}}(\mathit{\tau})}\langle\mathit{v},\nabla_{\mathit{t}}\rangle$ is a solution to Equation (10.2).

    Proof.

    Recall that

    $\begin{matrix} {\mathcal{C}_{\mathit{k}}^{\mathit{\sigma}}(\mathit{\tau}) = {conv}\left\{ \mathcal{W} \in \mathbb{R}^{\mathit{n} \times \mathit{m}} \mid \text{rank}(\mathcal{W}) \leq \mathit{k},\left\| \mathit{\sigma}(\mathcal{W}) \right\|_{2} \leq \mathit{\tau} \right\}.} \\ \end{matrix}$

    Let 𝒲 be some minimizer. Note that rescaling a matrix by a scalar has no effect on its rank. Let us hence assume that ∥σ(𝒲)∥2 = α for some α > 0 and characterize $\mathcal{W} \in \operatorname{arg\, min}_{\text{rank}(\mathit{v}) \leq \mathit{k}}\langle\mathit{v},\nabla_{\mathit{t}}\rangle$. Again, we have

    (10.9)$\begin{matrix} {{\langle\mathcal{W},\nabla_{\mathit{t}}\rangle}_{\mathit{F}} = \left\langle \overset{\leftarrow}{\mathcal{W}},\overset{\leftarrow}{\nabla_{\mathit{t}}} \right\rangle_{2} = \mathit{\alpha}\left\| \overset{\leftarrow}{\nabla_{\mathit{t}}} \right\|_{2}\cos\left( \angle\left( \overset{\leftarrow}{\mathcal{W}},\overset{\leftarrow}{\nabla_{\mathit{t}}} \right) \right),} \\ \end{matrix}$

    where $\overset{\leftarrow}{\mathit{x}}$ is there vectorized form of matrix x. Since we can choose α ≤ τ, this term is minimal as soon as the angle $\angle(\overset{\leftarrow}{\mathcal{W}},\overset{\leftarrow}{\nabla_{\mathit{t}}})$ is maximal, that is, $\cos(\angle(\overset{\leftarrow}{\mathcal{W}},\overset{\leftarrow}{\nabla_{\mathit{t}}})) < 0$ and α = τ, where we use the same Euclidean-geometric interpretation as in the proof for Lemma 10.3 above. To obtain a maximal angle, we hence minimize the l2-distance between $- \overset{\leftarrow}{\mathcal{W}}$ and $\overset{\leftarrow}{\nabla_{\mathit{t}}}$ in compliance with the rank constraint. Since again ${\| - \overset{\leftarrow}{\mathcal{W}} - \overset{\leftarrow}{\nabla_{\mathit{t}}}\|}_{2} = {\| - \mathcal{W} - \nabla_{\mathit{t}}\|}_{\mathit{F}}$, the Eckart–Young–Mirsky theorem yields the claim, where we rescale appropriately to meet the Schattennorm constraint.  □

    A.5 Convergence of SFW with gradient rescaling

    Before proving the convergence of SFW with gradient rescaling as stated informally in Theorem 10.2, we first recall some central definitions and assumptions.

    A.5.1 Setting

    Let Ω be the set of training datapoints from which we sample uniformly at random. In Equation (10.1), we defined a unique loss function ℓi for each datapoint. In the following, let ℓ(θ, ωi) = ℓi(θ) for ωi ∈ Ω. Similar to Reddi et al. [60] and Pokutta et al. [57], we define the SFW algorithm as in Algorithm 10.1, where the output θa is chosen uniformly at random from all iterates θ0, …, θT − 1.

    Let us recall some definitions. We denote the globally optimal solution by θ⋆ and the Frank–Wolfe Gap at θ as

    (10.10)$\begin{matrix} {\mathcal{G}(\mathit{\theta}) = \max\limits_{\mathit{v} \in \mathcal{C}}\left\langle \mathit{v} - \mathit{\theta}, - \nabla\mathit{L}(\mathit{\theta}) \right\rangle.} \\ \end{matrix}$

    We will use the same assumptions as Reddi et al. [60]. First of all, let us assume that L is M-smooth, that is,

    (10.11)$\begin{matrix} {\left\| \nabla\mathit{L}(\mathit{x}) - \nabla\mathit{L}(\,\mathit{y}) \right\| \leq \mathit{M}\|\mathit{x} - \mathit{y}\|} \\ \end{matrix}$

    for all x, y ∈ 𝒞, which implies the well-known inequality

    (10.12)$\begin{matrix} {\mathit{L}(\mathit{x}) \leq \mathit{L}(\,\mathit{y}) + \left\langle \nabla\mathit{L}(\,\mathit{y}),\mathit{x} - \mathit{y} \right\rangle + \frac{\mathit{M}}{2}\|\mathit{x} - \mathit{y}\|^{2}.} \\ \end{matrix}$

    Further, we assume the function ℓ to be G-Lipschitz, that is, for all x ∈ 𝒞 and ω ∈ Ω we have

    (10.13)$\begin{matrix} {\left\| \nabla\ell(\mathit{x},\mathit{\omega}) \right\| \leq \mathit{G}.} \\ \end{matrix}$

    A direct consequence is that the norm of the gradient estimator can be bounded as $\|\widetilde{\nabla}\mathit{L}(\mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{t}})\| \leq \mathit{G}$.

    A.5.2 Convergence proof

    The following well-established lemma quantifies how closely $\widetilde{\nabla}\mathit{L}(\mathit{\theta})$ approximates ∇L(θ). A proof can be found in Reddi et al. [60].

    Lemma 10.5.

    Let ω1, …, ωb be i. i. d. samples in Ω, θ ∈ 𝒞, and $\widetilde{\nabla}\mathit{L}(\mathit{\theta}) = \frac{1}{\mathit{b}}\sum_{\mathit{j} = 1}^{\mathit{b}}\nabla\ell(\mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{t}},\mathit{\omega}_{\mathit{j}})$. If ℓ is G-Lipschitz, then

    (10.14)$\begin{matrix} {\left. \mathbb{E} \right\|\left. \widetilde{\nabla}\mathit{L}(\mathit{\theta}) - \nabla\mathit{L}(\mathit{\theta}) \right\| \leq \frac{\mathit{G}}{\mathit{b}^{1/2}}.} \\ \end{matrix}$

    In the following, we denote the gradient estimator at iteration t as $\nabla_{\mathit{t}}: = \widetilde{\nabla}\mathit{L}(\mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{t}})$ and the l2-diameter 𝒟(𝒞) as 𝒟. Let β ∈ ℝ satisfy

    (10.15)$\begin{matrix} {\mathit{\beta} \geq \frac{2\mathit{h}(\mathit{\theta}_{0})}{\mathit{M}\mathit{D}^{2}},} \\ \end{matrix}$

    for some given initialization θ0 ∈ 𝒞 of the parameters, where h(θ0) = L(θ0) − L(θ⋆) denotes the optimality gap of θ0.

    Theorem 10.6. For all 0 ≤ t < T, let bt = b = T and ηt = ∥∇t∥η where $\mathit{\eta} = {(\frac{\mathit{h}(\mathit{\theta}_{0})}{\mathit{T}\mathit{M}\mathit{D}^{2}\mathit{G}^{2}\mathit{\beta}})}^{1/2}$. If θa is chosen uniformly at random from the SFW iterates {θi : 0 ≤ i < T}, then we have
    $\begin{matrix} {\mathbb{E}\,\left\lbrack \mathcal{G}(\mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{a}}) \cdot \right\|\left. \nabla\mathit{L}(\mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{a}}) \right\|\rbrack \leq \frac{\mathit{D}}{\sqrt{\mathit{T}}}\left( \sqrt{\mathit{h}(\mathit{\theta}_{0})\mathit{M}\mathit{G}^{2}\mathit{\beta}} + \mathit{G}^{2} + \frac{\mathit{M}\mathit{G}\mathit{D}}{2\sqrt{2}} \right),} \\ \end{matrix}$
    where 𝔼 denotes the expectation w. r. t. all the randomness present.
    Proof.

    First of all, notice that ηt is well-defined: Using β as defined above, we have

    (10.16)$\begin{matrix} {\mathit{\eta} \leq \left( \frac{1}{2\mathit{T}\mathit{G}^{2}} \right)^{1/2} = \frac{1}{\mathit{G}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\mathit{T}}},} \\ \end{matrix}$

    and consequently, we obtain $\mathit{\eta}_{\mathit{t}} = \|\nabla_{\mathit{t}}\|\mathit{\eta} \leq \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\mathit{T}}} \leq 1$ by using that ∥∇t∥ ≤ G. By M-smoothness of L, we have

    $\begin{matrix} {\mathit{L}(\mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{t} + 1})} & {\leq \mathit{L}(\mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{t}}) + \left\langle \nabla\mathit{L}(\mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{t}}),\mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{t} + 1} - \mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{t}} \right\rangle + \frac{\mathit{M}}{2}\|\mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{t} + 1} - \mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{t}}\|^{2}.} \\ \end{matrix}$

    Using the fact that θt + 1 = θt + ηt(vt − θt) and that ∥vt − θt∥ ≤ D, it follows that

    (10.17)$\begin{matrix} {\mathit{L}(\mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{t} + 1}) \leq \mathit{L}(\mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{t}}) + \mathit{\eta}_{\mathit{t}}\left\langle \nabla\mathit{L}(\mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{t}}),\mathit{v}_{\mathit{t}} - \mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{t}} \right\rangle + \frac{\mathit{M}\mathit{D}^{2}\mathit{\eta}_{\mathit{t}}^{2}}{2}.} \\ \end{matrix}$

    Now let

    (10.18)$\begin{matrix} {{\widehat{\mathit{v}}}_{\mathit{t}} = \operatorname{arg\, min}\limits_{\mathit{v} \in \mathcal{C}}\left\langle \nabla\mathit{L}(\mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{t}}),\mathit{v} \right\rangle = \operatorname{arg\, max}\limits_{\mathit{v} \in \mathcal{C}}\left\langle - \nabla\mathit{L}(\mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{t}}),\mathit{v} \right\rangle} \\ \end{matrix}$

    be the LMO solution if we knew the exact gradient at iterate θt, where t = 0, …, T − 1. This minimizer is not part of the algorithm but is crucial in the subsequent analysis. Note that we have

    (10.19)$\begin{matrix} {\mathcal{G}(\mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{t}}) = \max\limits_{\mathit{v} \in \mathcal{C}}\left\langle \mathit{v} - \mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{t}}, - \nabla\mathit{L}(\mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{t}}) \right\rangle = \left\langle {\widehat{\mathit{v}}}_{\mathit{t}} - \mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{t}}, - \nabla\mathit{L}(\mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{t}}) \right\rangle.} \\ \end{matrix}$

    Continuing from Equation (10.17), we therefore have

    $\begin{matrix} {\mathit{L}(\mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{t} + 1})} & {\leq \mathit{L}(\mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{t}}) + \mathit{\eta}_{\mathit{t}}\left\langle \widetilde{\nabla}\mathit{L}(\mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{t}}),\mathit{v}_{\mathit{t}} - \mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{t}} \right\rangle + \mathit{\eta}_{\mathit{t}}\left\langle \nabla\mathit{L}(\mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{t}}) - \widetilde{\nabla}\mathit{L}(\mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{t}}),\mathit{v}_{\mathit{t}} - \mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{t}} \right\rangle + \frac{\mathit{M}\mathit{D}^{2}\mathit{\eta}_{\mathit{t}}^{2}}{2}} \\ & {\leq \mathit{L}(\mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{t}}) + \mathit{\eta}_{\mathit{t}}\left\langle \widetilde{\nabla}\mathit{L}(\mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{t}}),{\widehat{\mathit{v}}}_{\mathit{t}} - \mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{t}} \right\rangle + \mathit{\eta}_{\mathit{t}}\left\langle \nabla\mathit{L}(\mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{t}}) - \widetilde{\nabla}\mathit{L}(\mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{t}}),\mathit{v}_{\mathit{t}} - \mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{t}} \right\rangle + \frac{\mathit{M}\mathit{D}^{2}\mathit{\eta}_{\mathit{t}}^{2}}{2}} \\ & {= \mathit{L}(\mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{t}}) + \mathit{\eta}_{\mathit{t}}\left\langle \nabla\mathit{L}(\mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{t}}),{\widehat{\mathit{v}}}_{\mathit{t}} - \mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{t}} \right\rangle + \mathit{\eta}_{\mathit{t}}\left\langle \nabla\mathit{L}(\mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{t}}) - \widetilde{\nabla}\mathit{L}(\mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{t}}),\mathit{v}_{\mathit{t}} - {\widehat{\mathit{v}}}_{\mathit{t}} \right\rangle + \frac{\mathit{M}\mathit{D}^{2}\mathit{\eta}_{\mathit{t}}^{2}}{2}} \\ & {= \mathit{L}(\mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{t}}) - \mathit{\eta}_{\mathit{t}}\,\mathcal{G}(\mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{t}}) + \mathit{\eta}_{\mathit{t}}\left\langle \nabla\mathit{L}(\mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{t}}) - \widetilde{\nabla}\mathit{L}(\mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{t}}),\mathit{v}_{\mathit{t}} - {\widehat{\mathit{v}}}_{\mathit{t}} \right\rangle + \frac{\mathit{M}\mathit{D}^{2}\mathit{\eta}_{\mathit{t}}^{2}}{2},} \\ \end{matrix}$

    where the first inequality is just a reformulation of Equation (10.17) and the second one is due to the minimality of vt. Applying Cauchy–Schwarz and using the fact that the diameter of 𝒞 is D, we therefore have

    (10.20)$\begin{matrix} {\left. \mathit{L}(\mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{t} + 1}) \leq \mathit{L}(\mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{t}}) - \mathit{\eta}_{\mathit{t}}\,\mathcal{G}(\mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{t}}) + \mathit{\eta}_{\mathit{t}}\mathit{D} \right\|\left. \nabla\mathit{L}(\mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{t}}) - \widetilde{\nabla}\mathit{L}(\mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{t}}) \right\| + \frac{\mathit{M}\mathit{D}^{2}\mathit{\eta}_{\mathit{t}}^{2}}{2}.} \\ \end{matrix}$

    Now note that ηt = ∥∇t∥η ≤ Gη, yielding

    (10.21)$\begin{matrix} {\left. \mathit{L}(\mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{t} + 1}) \leq \mathit{L}(\mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{t}}) - \mathit{\eta}_{\mathit{t}}\,\mathcal{G}(\mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{t}}) + \mathit{\eta}\mathit{G}\mathit{D} \right\|\left. \nabla\mathit{L}(\mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{t}}) - \widetilde{\nabla}\mathit{L}(\mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{t}}) \right\| + \frac{\mathit{M}\mathit{D}^{2}\mathit{G}^{2}\mathit{\eta}^{2}}{2}.} \\ \end{matrix}$

    Let θ0 : t denote the sequence θ0, …, θt. Taking expectations and applying Lemma 10.5, we get

    (10.22)$\begin{matrix} {\mathbb{E}_{\mathit{\theta}_{0:\mathit{t} + 1}}\mathit{L}(\mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{t} + 1}) \leq \mathbb{E}_{\mathit{\theta}_{0:\mathit{t} + 1}}\mathit{L}(\mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{t}}) - \,\mathbb{E}_{\mathit{\theta}_{0:\mathit{t} + 1}}\left\lbrack \mathit{\eta}_{\mathit{t}}\mathcal{G}(\mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{t}}) \right\rbrack + \frac{\mathit{D}\mathit{G}^{2}\mathit{\eta}}{\mathit{b}^{1/2}} + \frac{\mathit{M}\mathit{D}^{2}\mathit{G}^{2}\mathit{\eta}^{2}}{2}.} \\ \end{matrix}$

    By rearranging and summing over t = 0, …, T − 1, we get the upper bound

    (10.23)$\begin{matrix} {\sum\limits_{\mathit{t} = 0}^{\mathit{T} - 1}\mathbb{E}_{\mathit{\theta}_{0:\mathit{t} + 1}}\left\lbrack \mathit{\eta}_{\mathit{t}}\mathcal{G}(\mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{t}}) \right\rbrack} & {\leq \mathit{L}(\mathit{\theta}_{0}) - \mathbb{E}_{\mathit{\theta}_{0:\mathit{T}}}\mathit{L}(\mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{T}}) + \frac{\mathit{T}\mathit{D}\mathit{G}^{2}\mathit{\eta}}{\mathit{b}^{1/2}} + \frac{\mathit{T}\mathit{M}\mathit{D}^{2}\mathit{G}^{2}\mathit{\eta}^{2}}{2}} \\ & {\leq \mathit{L}(\mathit{\theta}_{0}) - \mathit{L}\left( \mathit{\theta}^{\star} \right) + \frac{\mathit{T}\mathit{D}\mathit{G}^{2}\mathit{\eta}}{\mathit{b}^{1/2}} + \frac{\mathit{T}\mathit{M}\mathit{D}^{2}\mathit{G}^{2}\mathit{\eta}^{2}}{2}.} \\ \end{matrix}$

    Now fix t and apply the law of total expectation to reformulate

    (10.24)$\begin{matrix} {\mathbb{E}_{\mathit{\theta}_{0:\mathit{t} + 1}}\left\lbrack \mathit{\eta}_{\mathit{t}}\mathcal{G}(\mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{t}}) \right\rbrack = \mathbb{E}_{\mathit{\theta}_{0:\mathit{t}}}\mathbb{E}_{\mathit{\theta}_{0:\mathit{t} + 1}}\left\lbrack \mathit{\eta}_{\mathit{t}}\mathcal{G}(\mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{t}}) \mid \mathit{\theta}_{0:\mathit{t}} \right\rbrack = \mathbb{E}_{\mathit{\theta}_{0:\mathit{t}}}\left\lbrack \mathcal{G}(\mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{t}})\mathit{\eta} \cdot \mathbb{E}_{\mathit{\theta}_{0:\mathit{t} + 1}}\left\lbrack \|\nabla_{\mathit{t}}\|\mspace{430mu}|\mspace{430mu}\mathit{\theta}_{0:\mathit{t}} \right\rbrack \right\rbrack,} \\ \end{matrix}$

    where we exploited that once θ0 : t is available, 𝒢(θt) is not subject to randomness anymore. The expected norm of the gradient estimator given θt depends only on the uniform selection of samples, allowing us to exploit the unbiasedness of the estimator as well as the convexity of the norm ‖·‖ using Jensen’s inequality as follows:

    (10.25)$\begin{matrix} {\mathbb{E}_{\mathit{\theta}_{0:\mathit{t} + 1}}\left\lbrack \|\nabla_{\mathit{t}}\|\mspace{430mu}|\mspace{430mu}\mathit{\theta}_{0:\mathit{t}} \right\rbrack} & {= \mathbb{E}_{\mathit{\omega}}\left\lbrack \|\nabla_{\mathit{t}}\| \mid \mathit{\theta}_{0:\mathit{t}} \right\rbrack} \\ \end{matrix}$
    (10.26)$\begin{matrix} & {\left. \geq \right\|\left. \mathbb{E}_{\mathit{\omega}}\lbrack\nabla_{\mathit{t}} \mid \mathit{\theta}_{0:\mathit{t}}\rbrack \right\|} \\ \end{matrix}$
    (10.27)$\begin{matrix} & {\left. = \right\|\left. \frac{1}{\mathit{b}}\sum\limits_{\mathit{j} = 1}^{\mathit{b}}\mathbb{E}_{\mathit{\omega}_{\mathit{j}}}\nabla\ell(\mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{t}},\mathit{\omega}_{\mathit{j}}) \right\|} \\ \end{matrix}$
    (10.28)$\begin{matrix} & {\left. = \right\|\left. \nabla\mathit{L}(\mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{t}}) \right\|.} \\ \end{matrix}$

    Combining this with Equation (10.23), we obtain

    (10.29)$\begin{array}{r} {\mathit{\eta}\sum\limits_{\mathit{t} = 0}^{\mathit{T} - 1}\mathbb{E}_{\mathit{\theta}_{0:\mathit{t}}}\left\lbrack \mathcal{G}(\mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{t}}) \cdot \right\|\left. \nabla\mathit{L}(\mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{t}}) \right\|\rbrack \leq \mathit{h}(\mathit{\theta}_{0}) + \frac{\mathit{T}\mathit{D}\mathit{G}^{2}\mathit{\eta}}{\mathit{b}^{1/2}} + \frac{\mathit{T}\mathit{M}\mathit{D}^{2}\mathit{G}^{2}\mathit{\eta}^{2}}{2}.} \\ \end{array}$

    Using the definition of θa, being a uniformly at random chosen iterate from θ0, …, θT − 1, we conclude the proof with the following inequality:

    (10.30)$\begin{matrix} {\mathbb{E}\,\left\lbrack \mathcal{G}(\mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{a}}) \cdot \right\|\left. \nabla\mathit{L}(\mathit{\theta}_{\mathit{a}}) \right\|\rbrack} & {\leq \frac{\mathit{h}(\mathit{\theta}_{0})}{\mathit{T}\mathit{\eta}} + \frac{\mathit{D}\mathit{G}^{2}}{\mathit{b}^{1/2}} + \frac{\mathit{M}\mathit{D}^{2}\mathit{G}^{2}\mathit{\eta}}{2}} \\ \end{matrix}$
    (10.31)$\begin{matrix} & {\leq \frac{\mathit{D}}{\sqrt{\mathit{T}}}\left( \sqrt{\mathit{h}(\mathit{\theta}_{0})\mathit{M}\mathit{G}^{2}\mathit{\beta}} + \mathit{G}^{2} + \frac{\mathit{M}\mathit{G}\mathit{D}}{2\sqrt{2}} \right)} \\ \end{matrix}$

     □

    Approximation of generalized frequency response functions via vector fitting

    Antonio Carlucci
    Ion Victor Gosea
    Stefano Grivet-Talocia

    Abstract

    This paper describes a method for data-driven approximation of nonlinear systems, using the notion of generalized frequency response functions as provided by the Volterra series theory. Using rational approximation, frequency-domain input–output data are fitted to a bilinear model structure. The proposed algorithm performs optimization of model coefficients through a greedy approach that relies on linear least-squares solves only, thus ensuring speed and scalability.

    Keywords: Volterra series, bilinear systems, vector fitting algorithm, generalized frequency response functions, least-squares fitting, Burgers’ equation,
    MSC 2020: 41A20, 93C10, 93C80,

    1 Introduction and background

    The Volterra series theory for nonlinear systems [21], [20] is a modeling approach based on expanding a given time-invariant input–output map y(t) = G[u(t)] using a series of generalized time-domain convolutions as

    (11.1)$\begin{matrix} {\mathit{y}(\mathit{t}) = \sum\limits_{\mathit{m} = 1}^{\infty}\int\limits_{0}^{\mathit{t}}\mathit{h}_{\mathit{m}}(\mathit{\tau}_{1},\ldots,\mathit{\tau}_{\mathit{m}})\mathit{u}(\mathit{t} - \mathit{\tau}_{1})\cdots\mathit{u}(\mathit{t} - \mathit{\tau}_{\mathit{m}})\text{d}\mathit{\tau}_{1}\ldots\text{d}\mathit{\tau}_{\mathit{m}},} \\ \end{matrix}$

    where u(t) is the system’s input (vanishing for t < 0), while y(t) is the output. This paper focuses on single-input, single-output (SISO) systems, that is, u(t), y(t) ∈ ℝ are scalars. In (11.1), the output is decomposed as a sum of contributions ym(t) from homogeneous subsystems, whose response is given as a multidimensional convolution with the one-sided kernel hm(τ1, …, τm). This series expansion is typically used to model mildly nonlinear systems since it has local validity around an operating point (in this case, u(t) = 0) and it is ensured to be convergent if the amplitude of u(t) is sufficiently small (see [20], [5] for details). Equation (11.1) is not enough to uniquely define the kernels hm, since different choices can describe the same input–output relation. Requiring that the hm’s are symmetric, that is, invariant under arbitrary permutations of the arguments, leads to a unique definition that is particularly convenient because they can be easily obtained analytically and measured from simulations. This formalism is valuable from a modeling standpoint because it generalizes the well-known convolution formula of linear systems, and allows defining generalized frequency response functions (GFRFs) through the multivariate Laplace transform [10]

    (11.2)$\begin{matrix} {\mathit{H}_{\mathit{m}}(\mathit{s}_{1},\ldots,\mathit{s}_{\mathit{m}}) = \int\limits_{0}^{\infty}\!\cdots\int\limits_{0}^{\infty}\mathit{h}_{\mathit{m}}(\mathit{\tau}_{1},\ldots,\mathit{\tau}_{\mathit{m}})\mathit{e}^{- \sum_{\mathit{i} = 1}^{\mathit{m}}\mathit{s}_{\mathit{i}}\mathit{\tau}_{\mathit{i}}}\text{d}\mathit{\tau}_{1}\ldots\text{d}\mathit{\tau}_{\mathit{m}}} \\ \end{matrix}$

    where hm(τ1, …, τm) is the symmetric kernel and Hm(s1, …, sm) is also called the degree-m symmetric transfer function.

    The objective of this paper is to derive a dynamical model starting from sampled data of symmetric transfer functions Hm(s1, …, sm). To this aim, a particularly convenient choice of the model structure is that of bilinear systems. These can be represented with the following state-space form:

    (11.3)$\begin{matrix} {\overset{˙}{\mathit{x}}(\mathit{t}) = \mathit{A}\mathit{x}(\mathit{t}) + \mathit{N}\mathit{x}(\mathit{t})\mathit{u}(\mathit{t}) + \mathit{B}\mathit{u}(\mathit{t}),\quad\mathit{y}(\mathit{t}) = \mathit{C}\mathit{x}(\mathit{t}).} \\ \end{matrix}$

    Such systems can be also viewed as time-varying linear systems, by rewriting the state equation as $\overset{˙}{\mathit{x}}(\mathit{t}) = \bar{\mathit{A}}(\mathit{t})\mathit{x}(\mathit{t}) + \mathit{B}\mathit{u}(\mathit{t})$ with $\bar{\mathit{A}}(\mathit{t}) = \mathit{A} + \mathit{N}\mathit{u}(\mathit{t})$. Therefore, stability and other relevant properties can be deduced from the already existing theory for linear systems, and hence, the bilinear structure has proven very useful and tractable for modeling. It is also sufficiently general since a broad class of systems with analytic nonlinearities can be embedded into a bilinear representation, for example, through the Carleman linearization approach [7] as in [6]. Additionally, by imposing specific boundary conditions for PDEs as in [3], bilinear models can be derived after semidiscretization in the spatial domain. For bilinear systems, several model reduction (MOR) techniques have been described as an immediate extension of their linear counterpart. Intrusive methods for MOR of bilinear systems, mostly based on moment matching (rational Krylov approaches) or balancing, were proposed in [6], [3] (see also the references therein), together with optimality-enforced methods and matching of infinite series [23], [2], [13]. Then data-driven approaches were also proposed, starting with a direct extension of the Loewner framework to bilinear systems in [1], and with more recent work in [16] that uses time-domain data to infer values of (symmetric) transfer functions; the latter was extended to quadratic systems in [17]. Subspace identification techniques for bilinear systems were proposed in [12], while the problem of structure-preserving MOR was treated in [4]. This paper proposes a novel approach toward data-driven approximation of GFRFs based on rational fitting. We provide an extension of the vector fitting algorithm to the nonlinear setting, featuring a greedy strategy whereby a sequence of linear least-squares problems is solved to optimize the coefficients of a conveniently chosen bilinear model structure.

    This paper is organized as follows. The notation and the model structure are provided in Section 2. The core ideas for fitting GFRFs are introduced in Section 2.1, followed by a discussion on the relation between the fitting error and the input–output response in Section 2.2. Then algorithmic tools for rational approximation based on Vector Fitting (VF) are reviewed and adapted in Section 2.3. Two numerical experiments are studied and the results are reported in Section 3, before concluding with Section 4.

    2 Formulation

    In order to introduce the problem data, let us use the shorthand sm ≜ (s1, …, sm) to denote a point in the m-dimensional frequency space. The starting point for model inference is thus a data set ℋ = {ℋm}m = 1M with evaluations of degree-m transfer functions at an arbitrary set of points

    (11.4)$\begin{array}{r} {\mathcal{H}_{\mathit{m}} = \left\{ \left( \mathbf{s}_{\mathit{m}}^{(\mathit{k})},{\breve{\mathit{H}}}_{\mathit{m}}^{(\mathit{k})} \right),\,\mathit{k} = 1,\ldots,\mathit{K}_{\mathit{m}} \right\},\quad\mathit{m} = 1,\ldots,\mathit{M}.} \\ \end{array}$

    This data is fitted with a predefined model structure corresponding to a particular bilinear dynamical system G with the following form:

    (11.5)$\begin{array}{r} {\mathit{G}:\,\left\{ \begin{array}{l} {{\overset{˙}{\mathit{x}}}_{1}(\mathit{t}) = \mathit{A}_{1}\mathit{x}_{1}(\mathit{t}) + \mathit{B}_{1}\mathit{u}(\mathit{t}),\quad} \\ {{\overset{˙}{\mathit{x}}}_{\mathit{m}}(\mathit{t}) = \mathit{A}_{\mathit{m}}\mathit{x}_{\mathit{m}}(\mathit{t}) + \mathit{N}_{\mathit{m}}\mathit{x}_{\mathit{m} - 1}(\mathit{t})\mathit{u}(\mathit{t}),\quad 2 \leq \mathit{m} \leq \mathit{M},\quad} \\ {\mathit{y}(\mathit{t}) = \sum_{\mathit{m} = 1}^{\mathit{M}}\mathit{C}_{\mathit{m}}\mathit{x}_{\mathit{m}}(\mathit{t}).\quad} \\ \end{array} \right.} \\ \end{array}$

    This was introduced in [20] as a way to construct bilinear realizations of Volterra transfer functions. Its structure is such that all kernels beyond the first M are zero, implying that G is a polynomial system of degree M (i. e., the sum in (11.1) contains M terms). In addition, state equations corresponding to every individual m in (11.5) correspond to the mth degree homogeneous subsystem of G [20], that is, the mth term in (11.1). The system (11.5) can be interpreted as a cascade of linear systems with a multiplicative nonlinearity in between. Denoting with Hm(k) the symmetric transfer functions of G evaluated at sm(k), the model coefficients should be optimized so that Hm is close to ${\breve{\mathit{H}}}_{\mathit{m}}$, that is, $\mathit{H}_{\mathit{m}}^{(\mathit{k})} \approx {\breve{\mathit{H}}}_{\mathit{m}}^{(\mathit{k})}$.

    It is to be mentioned that G in (11.5) could be recast into a standard bilinear system format as in (11.3). The way to do this is as suggested by the realization procedure in [20], that is, by putting together the bilinear system matrices (A, B, C, N), as follows:

    (11.6)$\begin{matrix} {\mathit{A} = \text{blkdiag}\{\mathit{A}_{1},\ldots,\mathit{A}_{\mathit{M}}\},\quad\mathit{B} = \text{col}\{\mathit{B}_{1},0,\ldots,0\},} \\ {\mathit{N} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & & & \\ \mathit{N}_{2} & 0 & & \\ & \mathit{N}_{3} & 0 & \\ & & \ddots & \ddots \\ \end{pmatrix},\quad\mathit{C} = \begin{pmatrix} \mathit{C}_{1} & \cdots & \mathit{C}_{\mathit{M}} \\ \end{pmatrix}.} \\ \end{matrix}$

    Different from [16], where the matrix N of the fitted bilinear system is computed to match the realization (A, B, C) computed with the Loewner framework in the first step, here we construct individual submodels (Am, Nm, Cm) at each step m ≥ 2. If necessary, these submodels may be assembled into a standard bilinear system, by following (11.6).

    2.1 Fitting of symmetric transfer functions

    The symmetric transfer functions of (11.5) can be expressed recursively. Starting from m = 1, let us define the auxiliary functions

    (11.7)$\begin{matrix} {\mathit{X}_{1}(\mathit{s}_{1})} & {= {(\mathit{s}_{1}\mathit{I} - \mathit{A}_{1})}^{- 1}\mathit{B}_{1},} \\ \end{matrix}$
    (11.8)$\begin{matrix} {\mathit{X}_{\mathit{m}}(\mathbf{s}_{\mathit{m}})} & {= \left\lbrack (\mathit{s}_{1} + \cdots + \mathit{s}_{\mathit{m}})\mathit{I} - \mathit{A}_{\mathit{m}} \right\rbrack^{- 1}\mathit{N}_{\mathit{m}}\mathit{Q}_{\mathit{m}}(\mathbf{s}_{\mathit{m}}),\quad\mathit{m} \geq 2,} \\ \end{matrix}$
    (11.9)$\begin{matrix} {\mathit{Q}_{\mathit{m}}(\mathbf{s}_{\mathit{m}})} & {= \sum\limits_{\mathit{i} = 1}^{\mathit{M}}\mathit{X}_{\mathit{m} - 1}(\mathbf{s}_{\mathit{m}}\backslash\mathit{s}_{\mathit{i}}),} \\ \end{matrix}$

    with sm ∖ si ≜ (s1, …, si − 1, si + 1, …, sm). The symmetric transfer functions become Hm(sm) = CmXm(sm), with the explicit formulation below:

    (11.10)$\begin{array}{r} {\mathit{H}_{\mathit{m}}(\mathbf{s}_{\mathit{m}}) = \left\{ \begin{matrix} {\mathit{C}_{1}{(\mathit{s}_{1}\mathit{I} - \mathit{A}_{1})}^{- 1}\mathit{B}_{1},\quad} & {\mathit{m} = 1,} \\ {\frac{1}{\mathit{m}!}\mathit{C}_{\mathit{m}}{\lbrack(\mathit{s}_{1} + \cdots + \mathit{s}_{\mathit{m}})\mathit{I} - \mathit{A}_{\mathit{m}}\rbrack}^{- 1}\mathit{N}_{\mathit{m}}\mathit{Q}_{\mathit{m}}(\mathbf{s}_{\mathit{m}}),\quad} & {\mathit{m} \geq 2.} \\ \end{matrix} \right.} \\ \end{array}$

    Expressions (11.9)–(11.10) can be easily derived for the assumed system structure (11.5) by applying the so-called growing exponential approach; see [20].

    In principle, the approximation problem we need to solve is to find model parameters so that the following cost function is minimized:

    (11.11)$\begin{matrix} {\mathit{J} = \sum\limits_{\mathit{m} = 1}^{\mathit{M}}\sum\limits_{\mathit{k} = 1}^{\mathit{K}_{\mathit{m}}}\left| \mathit{H}_{\mathit{m}}\left( \mathit{s}_{\mathit{m}}^{(\mathit{k})} \right) - {\breve{\mathit{H}}}_{\mathit{m}}\left( \mathit{s}_{\mathit{m}}^{(\mathit{k})} \right) \right|^{2}.} \\ \end{matrix}$

    Our approach is to greedily optimize individual terms of the summation corresponding to each m. Starting from m = 1, we consider the approximation

    (11.12)$\begin{array}{r} {\mathit{C}_{1}\left( \mathit{s}_{1}^{(\mathit{k})}\mathit{I} - \mathit{A}_{1} \right)^{- 1}\mathit{B}_{1} \approx {\breve{\mathit{H}}}_{1}\left( \mathit{s}_{1}^{(\mathit{k})} \right),\quad\mathit{k} = 1,\ldots,\mathit{K}_{1},} \\ \end{array}$

    that is equivalent to fitting a univariate rational function to given data, a problem known as rational fitting and efficiently solvable using existing algorithms, such as AAA [19] or vector fitting [15].

    As for m > 1, the recursive expression in (11.10) clearly shows the main idea of our formulation, based on observing that the mth degree transfer function is the product of a univariate transfer function

    (11.13)$\begin{matrix} {\mathit{F}_{\mathit{m}}(\mathit{s}) = \frac{1}{\mathit{m}!}\mathit{C}_{\mathit{m}}{(\mathit{s}\mathit{I} - \mathit{A}_{\mathit{m}})}^{- 1}\mathit{N}_{\mathit{m}},} \\ \end{matrix}$

    evaluated at s = s1 + ⋯ + sm with the function Qm(sm), which only depends on lower-degree subsystems. This implies that, if the system coefficients A1, …, Am and B1, N2, …, Nm are known up to index m, the quantity Qm(sm) is entirely determined. Therefore, the approximation problem is reduced to optimizing the coefficients of Fm(s) for each higher-degree index m = 2, …, M so that

    (11.14)$\begin{matrix} {\mathit{F}_{\mathit{m}}\left( \mathit{s}_{1}^{(\mathit{k})} + \cdots + \mathit{s}_{\mathit{m}}^{(\mathit{k})} \right)\mathit{Q}\left( \mathbf{s}_{\mathit{m}}^{(\mathit{k})} \right) \approx {\breve{\mathit{H}}}_{\mathit{m}}\left( \mathbf{s}_{\mathit{m}}^{(\mathit{k})} \right),\quad\mathit{k} = 1,\ldots,\mathit{K}_{\mathit{m}},} \\ \end{matrix}$

    which can be tackled again with rational fitting algorithms. The greedy aspect of this method lies in considering Q(sm(k)) a given constant as resulting from optimization of previous terms of the summation (11.11), rather than jointly optimizing all system parameters in (11.5) simultaneously.

    2.2 Cost function and model error

    The motivation for using J in (11.11) as a measure of model mismatch is that it works as a proxy for the H2 norm of the error system. In particular, using the notation ${\breve{\mathit{h}}}_{\mathit{m}}(\mathit{\tau}_{1},\ldots,\mathit{\tau}_{\mathit{n}})$ for the true Volterra kernels of the original system and hm(τ1, …, τn) for the fitted degree-M model, we can define the error $\mathit{e}_{\mathit{m}}(\mathit{\tau}_{1},\ldots,\mathit{\tau}_{\mathit{n}}) = \mathit{h}_{\mathit{m}}(\mathit{\tau}_{1},\ldots,\mathit{\tau}_{\mathit{n}}) - {\breve{\mathit{h}}}_{\mathit{m}}(\mathit{\tau}_{1},\ldots,\mathit{\tau}_{\mathit{n}})$. Following the definition in [23], [13], the H2 norm of the error system E would be

    (11.15)$\begin{array}{r} {\|\mathit{E}\|_{\mathit{H}_{2}} = \sqrt{\sum\limits_{\mathit{m} = 1}^{\infty}\|\mathit{e}_{\mathit{m}}\|_{2}^{2}},\quad\|\mathit{e}_{\mathit{m}}\|_{2}^{2} = \int\limits_{0}^{\infty}\cdots\int\limits_{0}^{\infty}\mathit{e}_{\mathit{m}}{(\mathit{\tau}_{1},\ldots,\mathit{\tau}_{\mathit{m}})}^{2}\mathit{d}\mathit{\tau}_{1}\cdots\mathit{d}\mathit{\tau}_{\mathit{m}}.} \\ \end{array}$

    Considering the magnitude of the output error $\mathit{e}(\mathit{t}) = \breve{\mathit{y}}(\mathit{t}) - \mathit{y}(\mathit{t})$,

    (11.16)$\begin{array}{r} \left| \mathit{e}(\mathit{t}) \middle| \leq \sqrt{\sum\limits_{\mathit{m} = 1}^{\mathit{M}}\|\mathit{e}_{\mathit{m}}\|_{2}^{2}}\sqrt{\sum\limits_{\mathit{m} = 1}^{\mathit{M}}\|\mathit{u}\|_{2}^{2\mathit{m}}} + \middle| \sum\limits_{\mathit{m} = \mathit{M} + 1}^{\infty}{\breve{\mathit{y}}}_{\mathit{m}}(\mathit{t}) \middle| . \right. \\ \end{array}$

    This estimate shows that the error contains two components, the first one depends on the modeling error of the first M kernels, while the second is the unmodeled nonlinearity of degree higher than M. The connection with the cost function J is made through Plancherel’s theorem to express ∥em∥22 in terms of the H2-norm of $\mathit{E}_{\mathit{m}}(\mathbf{s}_{\mathit{m}}) = \mathit{H}_{\mathit{m}}(\mathbf{s}_{\mathit{m}}) - {\breve{\mathit{H}}}_{\mathit{m}}(\mathbf{s}_{\mathit{m}})$,

    (11.17)$\begin{array}{r} {\sum\limits_{\mathit{m} = 1}^{\mathit{M}}\|\mathit{e}_{\mathit{m}}\|_{2}^{2} = \sum\limits_{\mathit{m} = 1}^{\mathit{M}}\frac{1}{{(2\mathit{\pi})}^{\mathit{m}}}\int\limits_{- \infty}^{\infty}\cdots\int\limits_{- \infty}^{\infty}\left| \mathit{E}_{\mathit{m}}(\mathit{j}\mathit{\omega}_{1},\ldots,\mathit{j}\mathit{\omega}_{\mathit{m}}) \right|^{2}\mathit{d}\mathit{\omega}_{1}\ldots\mathit{d}\mathit{\omega}_{\mathit{m}},} \\ \end{array}$

    and J can be viewed as a discrete analogue of the frequency-domain integrals.

    As for the choice of M, Equation (11.16) suggests that it should be chosen as the smallest degree for which the error due to the higher-degree responses ( m ≥ M + 1) are cumulatively negligible compared to the modeling error $\sum_{\mathit{m} = 1}^{\mathit{M}}\|\mathit{e}_{\mathit{m}}\|^{2}$ arising from the fitting procedure.

    2.3 Weighted vector fitting for GFRFs

    This section completes the formulation by describing the main enabling tool to solve the approximation problems (11.14) and (11.12), that is, the weighted vector fitting algorithm. In particular, (11.12) can be tackled with the standard formulation of VF [15], [11], [14]. On the other hand, (11.14) requires incorporating the arbitrary but known weighting vectors Q(sm(k)) using a modified formulation such as [8], here reviewed for the specific problem at hand. First of all, consider problem (11.14) for a particular m, restated as

    (11.18)$\begin{array}{r} {\text{minimize}\,\,\sum\limits_{\mathit{k} = 1}^{\mathit{K}}\left| \mathit{F}_{\mathit{m}}\left( \mathit{s}_{1}^{(\mathit{k})} + \cdots + \mathit{s}_{\mathit{m}}^{(\mathit{k})} \right)\mathit{Q}\left( \mathbf{s}_{\mathit{m}}^{(\mathit{k})} \right) - {\breve{\mathit{H}}}_{\mathit{m}}^{(\mathit{k})} \right|^{2},} \\ \end{array}$

    where Fm(s) is unknown and represented in pole-residue form as

    (11.19)$\begin{array}{r} {\mathit{F}_{\mathit{m}}(\mathit{s}) = \sum\limits_{\mathit{i} = 1}^{\mathit{\nu}}\frac{\mathit{R}_{\mathit{i}}}{\mathit{s} - \mathit{p}_{\mathit{i}}},} \\ \end{array}$

    with the index m being omitted in both the Ri’s and also the pi’s. Note that this pole-residue expansion is another way of parameterizing Fm(s) through coefficients Ri and pi, instead of the coefficients Cm, Am, Nm used in (11.13). However, it is always possible to write Fm(s) in the form (11.13) starting from the pole-residue (11.19), through a realization procedure (see [14]).

    Going back to the optimization problem in (11.18), a key observation is that if pi are given constants, (11.18) is an easily solvable linear least-squares (LS) problem in the variables Ri. However, if pi are to be optimized, this is no longer true and the problem becomes much harder. For this reason, VF goes through a preliminary pole identification phase to find poles pi through an iterated solution of a simplified problem. In this stage, a double barycentric form is used to represent Fm(s) as

    (11.20)$\begin{array}{r} {\mathit{F}_{\mathit{m}}(\mathit{s}) = \frac{\mathit{N}(\mathit{s})}{\mathit{d}(\mathit{s})},\quad\mathit{N}(\mathit{s}) = \sum\limits_{\mathit{i} = 1}^{\mathit{\nu}}\frac{\mathit{N}_{\mathit{i}}}{\mathit{s} - \mathit{q}_{\mathit{i}}},\quad\mathit{d}(\mathit{s}) = 1 + \sum\limits_{\mathit{i} = 1}^{\mathit{\nu}}\frac{\mathit{d}_{\mathit{i}}}{\mathit{s} - \mathit{q}_{\mathit{i}}},} \\ \end{array}$

    using a set of auxiliary poles {qi}i = 1ν. Starting from an initial guess of qi, this is updated through several iterations where the following modified cost function is minimized:

    (11.21)$\begin{array}{r} {\text{min}\,\,\sum\limits_{\mathit{k} = 1}^{\mathit{K}}\left| \mathit{N}\left( \mathit{s}_{1}^{(\mathit{k})} + \cdots + \mathit{s}_{\mathit{m}}^{(\mathit{k})} \right)\mathit{Q}\left( \mathbf{s}_{\mathit{m}}^{(\mathit{k})} \right) - {\breve{\mathit{H}}}_{\mathit{m}}^{(\mathit{k})}\mathit{d}\left( \mathit{s}_{1}^{(\mathit{k})} + \cdots + \mathit{s}_{\mathit{m}}^{(\mathit{k})} \right) \right|^{2}.} \\ \end{array}$

    Solving (11.21) at a given iteration yields coefficients di of d(s), that are used to update the auxiliary poles for the next iteration through the rule qi ← zeros{d(s)}. In this way, (11.21) is optimized repeatedly with an updated choice of qi each time. Upon convergence or after a maximum number of iterations, the qi’s are chosen to be the model poles pi in (11.19). Finally, (11.18) and (11.19) with fixed pi are solved via linear LS to find Ri.

    Convergence to a given set of poles qi corresponds to the condition d(s) → 1, detected either by checking whether the norm of coefficients $\sum_{\mathit{i} = 1}^{\mathit{\nu}}\mathit{d}_{\mathit{i}}^{2}$ falls below a predefined tolerance, or by looking at the maximum deviation |d(s) − 1|∞. Convergence of VF is discussed in [18], where it is shown that the algorithm might not converge in a strong sense. Nonetheless, VF still produces good solutions to the rational approximation problem, for which a globally optimal solution is hard to obtain due to the strongly nonconvex nature of the related optimization problem. In fact, thanks to its robustness and reliability, VF has become the method of choice in design automation tools and flows available on the market, in particular for electronic system design applications.

    The proposed algorithm for symmetric transfer function fitting is summarized as the pseudocode in Algorithm 11.1.

    3 Numerical examples and discussion

    3.1 Viscous Burgers’ equation

    This section reports on the example of the viscous Burgers’ equation

    (11.22)$\begin{array}{r} {\frac{\partial}{\partial\mathit{t}}\mathit{v}(\mathit{x},\mathit{t}) - \mathit{\nu}\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial\mathit{x}^{2}}\mathit{v}(\mathit{x},\mathit{t}) + \mathit{v}(\mathit{x},\mathit{t})\frac{\partial}{\partial\mathit{x}}\mathit{v}(\mathit{x},\mathit{t}) = 0,} \\ \end{array}$

    describing the velocity v(x, t) of a fluid in one spatial coordinate. The viscosity parameter was set to ν = 0.02. By following [6], the PDE was semi-discretized in space through a finite difference scheme with 200 points. The resulting nonlinear dynamical system describing the temporal evolution was formulated as a quadratic-bilinear system of size q = 200.

    A data-driven bilinear model with degree M = 2 could be constructed by sampling the first- and second-degree transfer functions H1(s1) and H2(s1, s2). In particular, H1(s1) was sampled on the imaginary axis at K1 = 200 points, log-spaced and corresponding to the frequency band [10 − 5, 800] Hz. The function H2(s1, s2) was sampled at K2 = 4964 points, with both s1 and s2 purely imaginary and in the frequency interval [10 − 5, 400] Hz. Running the proposed algorithm with ν = 8 poles, 40 iterations, and M = 2 to approximate H1 and H2 leads to a fitted bilinear model with overall order 13. Frequency-domain accuracy is reported in Figure 11.1, where the left panel shows the relative error with respect to both s1 and s2, and the right panel directly compares the responses.

    In the time domain, the responses of the full-order model are compared with the fitted one in Figure 11.2 (left panel). In this experiment, t ∈ [0, 10] s and the input is an amplitude-modulated chirp u(t) = 0.1cos [2πf0(t)t][1 − 1/2cos (2π2t)], with f0(t) sweeping from 1 mHz to 10 Hz, in order to test accuracy over a broad frequency range. In the right panel of Figure 11.2, we also show that the system nonlinearity is being modeled correctly because adding the degree-2 subsystem leads to a substantial error reduction compared to a simple degree-1 approximation (where only H1 is fitted).

    3.2 Nonlinear RC ladder

    This example is an electrical network with nonlinear elements, originally introduced in [9]. In particular, it is an RC ladder circuit with diodes in parallel to resistors (see Figure 11.3). The input u(t) is a current source, while the output y(t) is the voltage at the first node.

    Diodes have an exponential characteristic so that the original state equation contains nonpolynomial nonlinearities. Therefore, starting from a model with q = 50 states, Carleman bilinearization was used to obtain a lifted bilinear model with qbil = 502 + 50. The resulting system is considered the starting point for applying the proposed data-driven modeling scheme.

    We sampled H1(s1) at K1 = 101 points on the imaginary axis s1 = j2πf1, with f1 ∈ [10 − 1, 102] in addition to s1(1) = 0. Regarding higher-order transfer functions, we randomly selected K2 = 343 and K3 = 101 points to sample H2(s1, s2) and H3(s1, s2, s3).

    Using the proposed algorithm with ν = 6 poles and 20 iterations leads to the accurate fitting of the first M = 3 frequency responses, as shown in Figure 11.4 for m = 2. In time-domain, the model was tested in a 2-s long simulation with amplitude-modulated chirp input $\mathit{u}(\mathit{t}) = 2 \cdot \sin\lbrack 2\mathit{\pi}\mathit{f}_{0}(\mathit{t})\mathit{t} + \mathit{\pi}/2\rbrack\lbrack 1 - \frac{1}{2}\cos(2\mathit{\pi}\mathit{t})\rbrack$, with f0(t) varying linearly from 0.5 Hz to 50 Hz.

    Figure 11.5 compares the original and reduced model responses, showing that adding higher-order transfer functions decreases the error and that the degree-3 model is sufficient to produce a response that is indistinguishable from the full-order model for this case. Note that the error curves depicted in Figure 11.5 are related to the time-domain simulation used for testing that involves an oscillatory signal. The input has here been chosen to push the system into a regime of nonlinear operation where the contribution from the higher-order transfer functions can be appreciated and, in particular, models with M = 1, 2 are insufficient, as shown in Figure 11.6.

    4 Conclusions

    To summarize, this work described a new algorithm for data-driven approximation of nonlinear input–output maps in the frequency domain, based on Volterra series. The method uses samples of the symmetric transfer functions, directly measurable from response evaluation, without requiring access to the first-principles description of the system to be modeled. Compared to previous work [16], this framework is flexible as it can approximate GFRFs beyond the second degree. The entire procedure is fast and scalable as it consists of a sequence of linear least-squares optimization problems, thanks to a greedy approach that provides simplicity in exchange for exact optimality. Future work could address this issue, by investigating extensions of this algorithm in which transfer functions are fitted simultaneously rather than sequentially.
